title: Hide the customer, keep the work
desc: Your routine meets personal data at 07:00 with nobody watching. One palette entry decides whether it branches on it, hides it, or puts the real values back.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can place a Privacy Shield step in a routine, pick the right mode, bind what it scans, wire its two ways out, and read what it reports when the detector could not look.

steps.title: The 07:00 run nobody is watching
steps.bodyMd:
Van Dijk Groep has a routine that reads last week's complaint e-mails, asks the AI for a summary, and files it. It runs on Monday at 07:00 — with no colleague reading along.

The organisation's Privacy Shield may already be watching that run: the org setting **Also protect routines** is on by default. But that is one policy for the whole organisation, applied somewhere you cannot see it. It can stop a message or swap values for placeholders — it cannot send *your* run down a different path, and it cannot be tuned for one step.

That is what the **Privacy Shield step** is for: the same detector, placed where you can see it and react to it.

steps.title: One entry, four modes
steps.bodyMd:
In the canvas palette, under **Flow control**, there is one entry: **Privacy Shield** — *"Check for personal data, hide it, or show the real values again"*.

Drop it and the panel's first question is **"What should this step do?"** with four buttons:

- **Check for personal data** — scan a value and send the run down one path or the other
- **Check and hide** — scan, branch on the answer, and replace what was found with placeholders
- **Hide personal data** — replace personal data with placeholders; the real values come back later
- **Show real values again** — put the real values back where a step still holds placeholders

A fresh drop starts on **Check for personal data**: it is the only mode that changes no data.

steps.title: Which mode does this job?
steps.instruction: Four things Van Dijk Groep wants from a routine. Pair each with the mode that does it.

pairs.left: The complaint mails go to the AI for a summary, and customer names must not reach the model.
pairs.note: Hiding swaps every detected value for a placeholder before the value travels on.

pairs.left: A document is about to be filed in a shared folder; if it holds personal data an alert must go out, otherwise the run just continues.
pairs.note: A check changes nothing — it only decides which way out the run takes.

pairs.left: The same scan should raise the alert AND hand the next step a copy with the names taken out.
pairs.note: One node, two ways out, and a hidden copy on output.text for the path that found something.

pairs.left: A table column still reads [email_1] because that value never came back through the run.
pairs.note: This mode does not scan at all: it looks placeholders up in the run's own vault.

steps.title: Two ways out, and what to do on the bad one
steps.bodyMd:
The two checking modes leave the node by **personal data** or by **clean** — wire your alert to the first one. The two other modes have a single way on, so switching mode changes the node's shape on the canvas; when a switch would cost you a connection the editor asks first and names the one it would remove.

Under **On personal data** there are two tick boxes:

- **Stop the run** — the run fails, and the failure says which categories were found.
- **Pass a masked copy on** — adds `output.masked`, with every value replaced by `[person]`. Irreversible: the original cannot be recovered from it.

That last one is the opposite of hiding, which mints placeholders the run can undo.

steps.question: Check and hide mints placeholders like [email_1]. How does that differ from ticking "Pass a masked copy on"?

choices.label: Masking writes [person] without a counter and cannot be undone; the placeholders a hide mints are reversible from the run's vault.
They are the same mechanism, written differently — both can be restored later in the run.
choices.feedback: A masked copy drops the counter on purpose, so two occurrences can no longer be linked and nothing can put the original back.

choices.label: Masking covers more categories than hiding does.
choices.feedback: Both work from the same scan and the same category list. The difference is reversibility, not coverage.

choices.label: A masked copy is what the clean way out carries.
choices.feedback: There is nothing to mask on the clean path. output.masked only appears when the scan actually found something.

steps.explanation: Masking is a one-way door for text you never want restored; hiding is a round trip, because the mapping is minted into the run's token vault.

steps.title: What you set, and what you inherit
steps.bodyMd:
**What to scan** (the label changes per mode — *What to scan and hide*, *What to hide it in*, *What to restore*) is the only required field. Pick a value from an earlier step; the panel offers **Text from previous steps** as one-click picks. An object is scanned whole.

Open **Advanced** and you can narrow, never widen:

- **Look for** (labelled **Hide** on a hide-only step) — chips for all 21 categories, such as Person Names, Email Addresses, IBAN Numbers. Nothing narrowed means "everything the organisation looks for". A step may look for *less* than the Privacy Shield does, never more.
- **Only report matches above** — a number between 0 and 1. Left empty it reads **inherited**, and a value below the organisation's threshold is ignored: it can only raise it.

steps.title: Build Van Dijk Groep's Monday briefing
steps.instruction: Pick the trigger, then drag in the steps this routine needs — in order, and no more than it needs.

scenarios.brief: "Every Monday at 07:00, take last week's complaint e-mails, let the AI write a five-line summary, and put that summary in our datatable. The mails are full of customer names and addresses, and the model must not see them."

options.label: On form submission
options.desc: Publish a form; every submission runs this

options.label: On a schedule
options.desc: Run at a fixed time, over and over

options.label: On webhook call
options.desc: Run when an HTTP request arrives

options.label: On app event
options.desc: Run when something happens in a connected app

feedback.manual: Somebody would have to remember every Monday at 07:00 — the brief asks for a fixed time, over and over.
feedback.form: Nobody submits anything here; the briefing is about mails that already arrived.
feedback.webhook: A webhook fires when an outside system calls in. Nothing outside knows it is Monday.
feedback.app_event: An app event fires per incoming mail, which would give you one briefing per complaint instead of one per week.

palette.label: Privacy Shield — Show real values again

feedback.reveal: Not needed here. The real values are put back automatically wherever the run uses a value again — an AI reply is exactly such a moment. Add this mode only for a value that never came back that way.
feedback.stop: Stopping is a choice you make on a checking step when personal data must not be there at all. Here it is expected — it simply must not reach the model.

steps.title: "Nothing found" is not "we could not look"
steps.bodyMd:
If the detector is missing or down, a checking step never quietly reports **clean**. It reports that it was degraded, and your organisation's failure mode decides which way out the run takes — an organisation that fails closed (the default) takes the personal-data path, so the alert still fires.

A step in **Hide personal data** mode is stricter still: rather than hand the next step the original while you believe it was hidden, it fails the run and says that it could not scan, so nothing was hidden. **Check and hide** does not hand the original on either — it leaves the hidden copy empty and reports why.

The panel warns you up front too, when the detector is not installed, not responding, or its model has not loaded. And a step with nothing bound fails rather than scanning an empty string and calling it clean.

steps.question: A run finished successfully, but the letter it generated opens with "Beste [person_5]". The routine hides the mail body, the AI writes the letter, and an Edit data step carries a field forward into the document. Where do you look?

choices.label: Add a Show real values again step on that carried-forward field, and read its unresolved count — a value carried forward never passed a point where the run restores.
The organisation's category list — Person Names must be switched off.
choices.feedback: The opposite: [person_5] exists precisely because names were detected and hidden. A category that is off produces no placeholder at all.

choices.label: The threshold — set "Only report matches above" higher and the placeholder goes away.
choices.feedback: The threshold decides what gets detected, not what gets restored. Raising it would hide less, not put values back.

choices.label: Nothing is wrong — placeholders in a finished document are normal.
choices.feedback: They read as ordinary text and look deliberate, which is why leftovers are counted and reported rather than left for a customer to find.

steps.explanation: Values come back on their own where the run takes them back in — an AI reply, a tool result. A value carried forward by another step, or written to a table, stays hidden until a Show real values again step restores it, and that step reports what it could not resolve.

steps.title: Try it before it is real
steps.bodyMd:
Dry-run the routine before you activate it. In a dry run a Privacy Shield block does not fail the run — it is downgraded to an annotation that says it *would* stop here, so you can see the branch you built without breaking the preview.

Two things to look at afterwards:

- Which way out the run took, and whether the step reported that it was degraded.
- For a hide, whether the next step really reads the hidden copy. Bind it to `output.text`, not to the original value — otherwise the model still sees the real name and nothing tells you.

steps.title: Put one in a routine
steps.instruction: Open a routine of yours (or make a new one), drag Privacy Shield out of the Flow control group, and pick a mode. Bind What to scan to a real value from an earlier step, then save. Do not activate anything you were not planning to run.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Pick the mode by the job**: check to branch, check and hide to do both, hide before the data travels on, show real values again only where a value never came back on its own.
- **Narrow, never widen**: Look for and Only report matches above can tighten the organisation's Privacy Shield for one step, never loosen it.
- **Read the honest answers**: a degraded scan is not a clean one, a masked copy is one-way, and leftover placeholders are counted and reported rather than hidden from you.

practiceTopic.title: The Privacy Shield step in routines
practiceTopic.summary: One palette entry with four modes that scans, branches, hides or restores personal data inside a routine.
facts: The Privacy Shield entry sits in the Flow control group of the step palette and reads "Check for personal data, hide it, or show the real values again".
The four modes are Check for personal data, Check and hide, Hide personal data and Show real values again; a fresh drop starts on the check, because it changes no data.
Only the two checking modes branch — the run leaves by personal data or by clean; hide and reveal have one way on.
On personal data offers Stop the run (the failure names the categories found) and Pass a masked copy on (output.masked, every value replaced by [person], irreversible).
Hiding mints reversible placeholders like [email_1], and the real values are put back automatically wherever the run uses a value again, such as an AI reply or a tool result.

Advanced holds Look for (21 categories, all of them unless you narrow; labelled Hide on a hide-only step) and Only report matches above (0 to 1, empty reads "inherited"); a step may only tighten the organisation's policy.

A detector that is missing or down produces a degraded result, never a clean one, and the organisation's failure mode decides the branch; a step in Hide personal data mode fails the run instead of passing the original on.
In a dry run a Privacy Shield block becomes a "would stop" annotation instead of a failure.

actionChecks.label: Add a Privacy Shield step to a routine
actionChecks.hint: In Studio → Routines, open or create a routine, drag Privacy Shield from the Flow control group onto the canvas, bind what it should scan, and save.

criteria.label: A routine of your own exists
criteria.hint: Open or create one in Studio → Routines. The Privacy Shield step and what it scans are stored inside the routine, where this check cannot look — the step on the canvas is your proof.
